text.p: Liberia's West African neighbours have given it the green light for presidential and parliamentary elections on May 30 to end over seven years of a brutal civil war.

West African foreign ministers overseeing the peace process said on Friday after two days of talks that their peacekeeping force ECOMOG would pull out six months after a new government is installed, leaving behind a new national army and police force.

In neighbouring Ivory Coast, a U.S. transport plane and troops arrived from Europe on Friday to airlift in over 1,000 extra West African peacekeepers to bolster the 10,000-strong force over the coming days, witnesses said.

"The time is short. This will require a lot of work, a lot of financial and logistics support which we hope will be found in time to ensure that this programme is carried through successfully," Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi said.

May 30 is the date envisaged under a peace accord brokered by leaders of Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) leaders in Nigeria's capital Abuja in August -- after a dozen earlier agreements collapsed.

Ikimi told a news conference the election would be organised by an electoral commission comprising seven Liberians and three international observers -- one from the Organisation of African Unity, one from the United Nations and one from ECOWAS.
Liberia's three main faction leaders will each name a representative with four members representing labour unions, women's groups, youth groups and political parties.

Ikimi, chairman of the ECOWAS ministerial committee on Liberia, said the commander of the Nigerian-led ECOWAS peacekeeping force was satisfied on the security front following the disarmament of faction fighters.

General Victor Malu, he said, had reported "the successful conclusion of the disarmament and demobilisation exercise and that there were enough security guarantees to go ahead with the implementation of the entire Abuja accord as planned."

Liberia, founded by freed American slaves in 1847, has strong emotional links with the United States. U.S. helicopters airlifted out U.S. and other foreign nationals during a flare-up in the war in Monrovia last April and May.
Charles Taylor, who launched the war from Ivory Coast in late 1989, has already announced plans to stand for president. So has Alhaji Kromah, his sometime rival and sometime ally.

Ikimi said voting would be by proportional representation. "The proportional representation type of elections is necessary because the existing constituencies have been eroded by the seven years of civil war," he said.

He also said there would be no voting outside Liberia -- a contentious issue since hundreds of thousands of Liberians are camped in neighbouring countries, mainly Ivory Coast. "The refugees will be repatriated home to take part in the voting."

He gave no details on whether, when or how a census of voters would be held, but he said a new supreme court would be formed with ECOWAS ensuring its impartiality. The court will check the election results and rule on any disputes.
Well over 150,000 people, many of them civilians, have been killed in the civil war.
Ikimi said ECOMOG planned to train Liberians to replace it. "There will be a new armed forces, a new police force," he said, adding that all tribes and regions would be fully represented.
